title: Sequence modeling and design from molecular to genome scale with Evo

items.q: What is Evo?
items.a: Evo is a long-context genomic foundation model with 7 billion parameters, trained on millions of prokaryotic and phage genomes at single-nucleotide resolution.
items.info: It uses a frontier architecture (StripedHyena) and a context length of 131 kilobases.
items.concl: A single DNA model that generalizes across DNA, RNA and protein modalities.

items.q: What can Evo do according to the abstract?
items.a: Zero-shot function prediction competitive with domain-specific language models, generation of functional CRISPR-Cas and transposon systems, prediction of how small mutations affect whole-organism fitness, and generation of megabase-scale sequences with plausible genomic architecture.
items.info: The CRISPR-Cas and transposon generations are presented as the first examples of protein-RNA and protein-DNA codesign with a language model.
items.concl: Prediction and generation span molecular to genomic scales of complexity.

items.q: What gap in machine learning for biology does the paper address?
items.a: Existing models are modality-specific (proteins, coding sequences, RNA or regulatory DNA separately) and generative applications were limited to single molecules, simple complexes or short DNA sequences.
items.info: Complex processes such as gene regulation, CRISPR immunity or transposition rely on interactions involving molecules across multiple modalities.
items.concl: A DNA model unifying molecular, systems and genome scales could capture systems-wide interactions.

items.q: Why are Transformer architectures a problem for DNA language modeling?
items.a: Dense Transformers scale quadratically with input sequence length relative to model width and generally underperform at single-nucleotide (byte-level) resolution.
items.info: As a result, Transformer DNA models use short contexts and aggregate nucleotides into coarser tokens, sacrificing single-nucleotide resolution.

items.q: Why does single-nucleotide resolution matter biologically?
items.a: Because individual single-nucleotide mutations can completely alter organism function, so a model at that resolution can incorporate the evolutionary effects of fine-grained sequence variation.

items.q: What is the StripedHyena architecture used by Evo?
items.a: A hybrid of 29 layers of data-controlled convolutional operators (hyena layers) interleaved with 3 layers (10%) of multihead attention with rotary position embeddings (RoPE).
items.info: Evo has 32 blocks at a model width of 4096 dimensions; channel mixing uses gated linear units and inputs are normalized with root mean square layer normalization.

items.q: What do hyena layers do?
items.a: They process sequences in an input-dependent way using compositions of short and long convolution filters plus data-controlled gating, which filters noisy DNA patterns and aggregates individual nucleotides into motifs.
items.info: They are subquadratic in time and can be evaluated via Fast Fourier Transforms or parallel scans.

items.q: How does Evo compare with HyenaDNA?
items.a: Evo uses an improved hybrid design and is scaled to 1000 times larger model size and 100 times more data than HyenaDNA, a previous generation of Hyena-based DNA models.

items.q: What is OpenGenome?
items.a: The pretraining dataset: more than 80,000 bacterial and archaeal genomes plus millions of predicted phage and plasmid sequences, covering 300 billion nucleotide tokens.
items.info: Sources are GTDB v214.1 (bacteria and archaea), IMG/VR v4 (prokaryotic viruses) and IMG/PR (plasmids). GTDB contained 80,789 bacterial and 4,416 archaeal genomes.

items.q: Which sequences were deliberately excluded from pretraining and why?
items.a: Viral genomes that infect eukaryotic hosts were excluded for safety considerations.
items.info: Filtering kept only viruses found at least twice in a prokaryotic host, then removed 19 virus families and 12 orders, plus viruses with poor taxonomic specificity.

items.q: How is Evo trained, in terms of objective and stages?
items.a: By next-token prediction on raw genome sequences with no supervision or annotations, in a first stage with 8192-token context and a second context-extension stage with 131,072-token context.
items.info: Tokenization is single-nucleotide, byte-level (UTF-8), with an effective vocabulary of 4 tokens out of a total of 512 characters so extra tokens can be used for prompting.

items.q: What is perplexity and why is it used here?
items.a: Perplexity measures how well an autoregressive model predicts the next token of a sequence; a lower value is better and it correlates highly with downstream task performance.

items.q: Which architectures were compared in the DNA scaling laws analysis?
items.a: Transformer++, Mamba, Hyena and StripedHyena, with more than 300 models trained across the four architectures.
items.info: Transformer++ is a modern decoder-only Transformer with RoPE and SwiGLU; Mamba is a data-controlled state-space model.

items.q: What was the outcome of the scaling laws comparison?
items.a: Transformer++ had substantially worse perplexity at all compute budgets, while Hyena and StripedHyena had the best scaling rates; StripedHyena also trained stably at all sizes and learning rates.
items.info: Transformer++ and Mamba showed numerical instability and degraded more outside the compute-optimal frontier. This motivated choosing StripedHyena for Evo.
items.concl: First scaling laws analysis for large-scale DNA pretraining; models improve monotonically with scale.

items.q: Was Evo trained compute-optimally?
items.a: No. The compute-optimal number of tokens for Evo 7B was estimated at 250 billion, so training on 300 billion tokens meant a 17% offset from the compute-optimal model size in the 8192-context phase.
items.info: Performance outside the compute-optimal frontier matters in practice because most models are trained on more tokens than compute-optimal laws recommend.

items.q: What is a deep mutational scanning (DMS) study and how is it used to benchmark the model?
items.a: DMS introduces an exhaustive set of mutations into a coding sequence and experimentally measures fitness for each variant; the model's sequence likelihood (or pseudolikelihood) is correlated with those fitness scores as a zero-shot prediction.
items.info: For nucleotide models the wild-type coding sequence and nucleotide mutations from the original studies are used.

items.q: How did Evo perform on prokaryotic protein DMS datasets?
items.a: Evo's zero-shot performance exceeded all other nucleotide models tested, including GenSLM, and was competitive with leading protein-specific language models.
items.info: Nine prokaryotic protein DMS datasets were used. Evo was trained on genomic sequence with no explicit coding sequence annotations.
items.concl: Evo is already competitive with state-of-the-art protein language modeling on bacterial proteins.

items.q: Could Evo predict mutational effects in human proteins?
items.a: No, Evo was unable to predict mutational effects on fitness in human protein DMS datasets, most likely because its pretraining data is entirely prokaryotic.
items.info: There was a strong association between language-model perplexity on the wild-type sequence and fitness prediction performance, suggesting fine-tuning or pretraining on mammalian coding sequences could help.

items.q: How well did Evo predict mutational effects on noncoding RNA function?
items.a: Evo outperformed all other tested nucleotide language models, including RNA-FM, an RNA language model explicitly trained on ncRNA sequences, across seven ncRNA DMS datasets.
items.info: Strongest result: 5S rRNA mutations affecting E. coli growth rate, Spearman r = 0.60, two-sided t-distributed P = 1.9 x 10^-3.
items.concl: Evo learns functional information about tRNAs, rRNAs and ribozymes without RNA-specific training.

items.q: How well did Evo's zero-shot likelihoods predict promoter activity?
items.a: Mean Spearman r = 0.43 across four promoter studies, exceeding GC content (mean r = 0.35) and GenSLM zero-shot likelihoods (mean r = 0.09).
items.info: This was comparable to a CNN trained on one-hot embeddings (mean r = 0.44).
items.concl: Evo pretraining contains sequence-intrinsic information useful for promoter activity.

items.q: What did supervised models on Evo embeddings achieve?
items.a: A CNN trained on Evo embeddings reached mean Spearman r = 0.56, approaching Promoter Calculator, a state-of-the-art biophysical promoter model (mean r = 0.62).
items.info: The CNN beat ridge regression on both embedding types, and Evo embeddings beat one-hot embeddings for both model types; supervised models were trained on LaFleur et al. data and tested out of domain.

items.q: What happened when promoter and ribosome-binding site (RBS) sequences were combined?
items.a: Zero-shot prediction of protein expression improved from r = 0.17 (RBS alone) and r = 0.47 (promoter alone) to r = 0.61 for the concatenated promoter-RBS sequence.
items.info: This beat GC content (r = 0.47), GenSLM (r = 0.11) and RBS Calculator (r = 0.39). Data from Kosuri et al., ~12,000 promoter-RBS pairs in E. coli.
items.concl: Additional regulatory sequence provides useful functional context to the model.

items.q: Why should a genome model be able to codesign protein-RNA complexes?
items.a: In prokaryotes functionally related genes are organized into operons next to each other, so a model that learns covariation among genetic elements within its context window can learn protein-ncRNA interactions such as Cas protein and its crRNA.
items.info: For Cas9, a tracrRNA forms a duplex with the crRNA to make the full guide RNA.

items.q: How was Evo fine-tuned for CRISPR-Cas generation?
items.a: On 72,831 CRISPR-Cas loci of 8 kb extracted from public metagenomic and genomic sequences, with special prompt tokens for Cas9, Cas12 and Cas13 prepended to each training sequence.
items.info: Prompting with a given Cas token produced generations whose most common Cas protein matched that token. Fine-tuning from the base Evo model gave higher quality and more diverse generations than training only on CRISPR-Cas sequences.

items.q: How were generated Cas loci classified and filtered?
items.a: A generation counted as Cas9/Cas12/Cas13 if it had a CRISPR array detected by MinCED and an ORF with a positive hit to a Cas profile HMM at E value < 1 x 10^-3.
items.info: About 2 million generated sequences were filtered for Cas9 loci with RuvC and HNH domains, a CRISPR repeat array and a detectable tracrRNA; 11 systems with robust pLDDT were chosen for experimental validation.

items.q: What was EvoCas9-1 and how did it perform?
items.a: One of 11 tested Cas9 generations showed robust activity; purified EvoCas9-1 with its Evo-generated sgRNA had in vitro cleavage activity comparable to SpCas9 with its canonical sgRNA.
items.info: Tested with a DNA target containing an NGG PAM at a 10:10:1 molar ratio of Cas9:sgRNA:target, 1 nM target, with timepoints from 5 min to 3 hours.
items.concl: First protein-RNA codesign with a language model validated experimentally.

items.q: How novel was EvoCas9-1 in sequence terms?
items.a: Its amino acid sequence shares 79.9% identity with the closest Cas9 in the fine-tuning database and 73.1% identity with SpCas9; the designed sgRNA is 91.1% identical to the canonical SpCas9 sgRNA.
items.info: The sgRNA differs in the two terminal stem loops, extending stem loops 2 and 3; AlphaFold3 cofolding of protein, RNA and DNA gave a mean pLDDT of 90, and the predicted protein has a more positive surface charge than SpCas9.

items.q: What are IS200/IS605 mobile genetic elements?
items.a: A family of MGEs that spread by peel-and-paste transposition, catalyzed by the homodimeric transposase TnpA interacting with terminal hairpins at the left end (LE) and right end (RE) of the element.
items.info: The element is excised from single-stranded DNA as a circular product containing an RE-LE junction. IS605 elements additionally encode an RNA-guided TnpB nuclease with a cognate omega RNA.

items.q: What was the transposon fine-tuning set, and what did Evo learn about element boundaries?
items.a: Evo was fine-tuned on 10,720 IS605 elements and 219,866 IS200 elements in natural sequence context; positional entropy showed a sharp sustained increase at the 3' end of the element, indicating learned MGE boundaries.
items.info: A categorical Jacobian analysis showed the model uses information from one end to specify the other across ~1 to 2 kb, reflecting the evolutionary linkage of the two terminal elements.

items.q: What fraction of generated transposons worked in vitro?
items.a: 11 of 24 Evo-generated IS200-like elements and 3 of 24 IS605-like elements showed evidence for both excision and insertion in vitro, a success rate near 50% for IS200-like systems.
items.info: Activity depended on a putative catalytic tyrosine and on a ssDNA (not dsDNA) substrate, consistent with the known TnpA mechanism; nanopore sequencing of PCR products identified precise element boundaries.
items.concl: First protein-DNA codesign with a language model, validated experimentally.

items.q: How divergent were the functional transposon designs?
items.a: The 14 active elements use a diverse set of hairpins and encode functional TnpA proteins with sequence identity as low as 67% to the fine-tuning database.
items.info: Functional IS605-like generations also contained sequences matching a covariance model of known omega RNAs (cmsearch E value < 0.001). Example ISEvo2 TnpB was only 61% identical to training.

items.q: How did the authors test whether Evo learns gene essentiality?
items.a: By an in silico mutagenesis screen inserting premature stop codons at the beginning of each coding sequence of a genome and measuring the change in Evo log-likelihood versus the wild-type sequence.
items.info: Likelihoods were computed with gene-only context, 8k context (8192 tokens) or 66k context (65,536 tokens) of flanking genomic sequence.
items.concl: Hypothesis: mutating essential genes gives larger, more negative log-likelihood changes.

items.q: What were the gene essentiality results?
items.a: With 66k context the likelihood changes were significantly associated with essentiality (Bonferroni-corrected permutation P < 0.05) in 49 of 58 genomes.
items.info: Data were 56 bacterial essentiality studies from the DEG database plus two phage studies. Best cases: AUROC 0.90 for lambda phage and 0.84 for Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
items.concl: Evo learns how small mutations affect whole-organism fitness without annotations or task-specific training.

items.q: Did genomic context matter for essentiality prediction?
items.a: Yes. Performance improved substantially from gene-only context to 8k context; from 8k to 66k the average was comparable but the lower range of examples improved.
items.info: Controls: gene position in the genome showed no link to essentiality; sequence conservation was similar to Evo with gene-only context but weaker than Evo with genomic context. GenSLM showed no sensitivity to essentiality.
items.concl: The added value comes from Evo considering a gene within its broader genomic context.

items.q: How long were the genome-scale generations and how were they prompted?
items.a: Sixteen sequences of about 1 Mb (more than seven times the 131 kb context length) were sampled, four each from four bacterial species-level prompts, at temperature 1.0 and top-k 4.
items.info: Prompts were Greengenes-style lineage strings for Mycoplasma genitalium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli. The smallest minimal bacterial genomes are ~580 kb.

items.q: How natural did the generated megabase sequences look?
items.a: Coding densities were nearly the same as natural genomes and far above random sequence, with operon-like clusters of colocated genes on the same strand, and 128 tRNAs covering anticodons for all canonical amino acids across ~16 Mb.
items.info: CheckM was used for quality metrics; almost all ESMFold-predicted proteins had secondary structure and globular folds, many with GO molecular function matches.

items.q: What are tetranucleotide usage deviations (TUDs) and what did they show?
items.a: TUDs are a strong indicator metric of phylogenetic relatedness; generated sequences correlated strongly with their corresponding natural reference genomes (Pearson r = 0.53 to 0.88) and reproduced the natural phylogenetic relationships.
items.info: Stop codon usage also matched prokaryotic patterns (TGA and TAA most frequent, TAG least), unlike random sequences.
items.concl: Species-specific prompting works at the level of genome-wide compositional signatures.

items.q: What was unnatural about the generated genomes?
items.a: They lack many highly conserved marker genes typical of complete genomes, with only three rRNAs generated across ~16 Mb, and many predicted protein structures are low confidence, biased toward alpha-helical folds, with limited structural matches to natural proteins.
items.concl: The samples are a 'blurry image' of a genome: plausible high-level organization but lacking fine-grained detail.

items.q: What are the stated limitations of Evo?
items.a: It was pretrained on only 300 billion prokaryotic tokens (a minuscule fraction of available data), cannot predict human protein fitness effects, often produces problematic CRISPR-Cas generations with missing or truncated cas genes, and fails to include full sets of rRNAs at genome scale.
items.info: The authors compare these to the limitations of natural language models, which improved with scale, labeled data, prompt engineering and alignment.

items.q: How do the authors handle biosafety and ethics?
items.a: They excluded eukaryotic viruses from pretraining, open-sourced the model to promote transparency, and point to the GA4GH principles for oversight of genetic engineering technologies as a foundation for governance.
items.info: Code and models are at https://github.com/evo-design/evo, with pretrained and fine-tuned checkpoints on Hugging Face and OpenGenome publicly available.

items.q: What future directions do the authors propose?
items.a: More scale, longer context and more diverse pretraining data; language-model-guided directed evolution of multigene systems; better multigene structure prediction; semantic metagenomic mining; and incorporation of eukaryotic genomes.
items.info: They note eukaryotic genomes bring far higher complexity and need substantial investment in engineering, compute and safety-related alignment.

items.q: What compute was used to train Evo?
items.a: Stage 1 on 64 NVIDIA H100 GPUs for 2 weeks and stage 2 on 128 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for another 2 weeks, totalling ~340 billion tokens and ~2 x 10^22 FLOPs.
items.info: Since OpenGenome has 300B tokens this equals 1.13 epochs. Pipeline parallelism with 2 stages was used to cut memory footprint.

items.q: How was the context window extended from 8k to 131k?
items.a: By linear position interpolation of the rotary position embedding learned in the first 8k pretraining stage.
items.info: Other interpolation methods were tested but performed slightly worse on this data. Sequence packing with end-of-sequence tokens separating contigs was used for dataloading.

items.q: What hyperparameters were used for the CRISPR-Cas and IS200/IS605 fine-tuning?
items.a: Most pretraining hyperparameters were kept, with batch size set to 524,288 tokens and an initial learning rate of 0.00009698 (the final pretraining learning rate), fine-tuning for about 10 epochs.
items.info: The dataloader was modified so each training sample starts at the first token of the locus, padding shorter sequences without contributing to loss. Sampling swept temperatures 0.1 to 1.3 and top-k values of 2 and 4.

items.q: How were the CRISPR-Cas loci curated?
items.a: Profile HMMs for Cas9, Cas12 and Cas13 were searched with hmmsearch (-Z 1000000), keeping hits at E < 1 x 10^-6 that were at least 300 aa and covered over 80% of the pHMM, with CRISPR arrays detected by minced; only one locus per 90% identity Cas cluster was kept (MMseqs2 easy-cluster).
items.info: Loci were extracted with flanking sequence up to 8192 nucleotides. For IS200/IS605 the Pfam Y1 HUH transposase model PF01797 was used, keeping TnpA hits under 400 aa.

items.q: Which tools were used to evaluate generated sequences?
items.a: Prodigal for ORFs, CheckM for genome quality and coding density, tRNAscan-SE for tRNAs, barrnap for rRNAs, ESMFold and AlphaFold3 for structure, and FoldSeek against AlphaFold DB UniRef50 for structural matches.
items.info: A FoldSeek alignment was considered a structural match if the average of query and target TM-score exceeded 0.4; those matches transferred GO terms to Evo-generated proteins.

items.text: Zero-shot Evo likelihood of promoter plus RBS reached r = 0.61 for protein expression in E. coli. Worth checking whether the same promoter-plus-context framing helps when scoring enhancers or CREs in vertebrate genomes with eukaryote-trained successors.

Evo is prokaryote-only and explicitly fails on human protein DMS. Go back to how later eukaryotic genome models (e.g. Evo 2 / AlphaGenome-type models) handle the much larger noncoding fraction and whether context length alone is enough.
